items.detail: A third straight decline, and this time the small caps took the worst of it — the **S&P 500 fell 0.48% to 7,636.46**, the Dow dropped 0.77% to **52,381.02**, the Nasdaq lost 0.64% to 26,253.34 and the **Russell 2000 sank 1.30%**.
items.why: The oil story escalated from proxy strikes to a direct US-Iran naval exchange that pushed Brent through $100, and the 10-year yield hit its highest level since 2023, squeezing corporate margin and consumer-demand expectations at the same time.

items.detail: Crude finally cleared the round number — **Brent surged 3.4% to $101.21** and WTI climbed to roughly **$96.05**, a seventh consecutive advance.
items.why: US forces struck five Iranian tankers near Kharg Island, Iran's main export hub, and Tehran responded by claiming attacks on two American vessels and eight oil tankers in the Gulf, warning crews near Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports to abandon ship and firing ballistic missiles toward Jordan.

items.detail: The bond move was self-inflicted as much as oil-driven — the **10-year yield climbed to 4.841%, the highest since November 2023**, after Treasury tripled its long-end buyback to **up to $6 billion** and the market sold off anyway.
items.why: Wall Street had positioned for a $7 billion to $10 billion operation, so a $6 billion figure read as Scott Bessent lacking the firepower to lean against the market, and yields rose on the announcement instead of falling.

items.detail: Apple's biggest product day of the year landed with a shrug — the stock **slipped about 1%** through Wednesday afternoon after the 'Surprise and Shine' event unveiled the **iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the foldable iPhone Duo, new Apple Watches and AirPods 5**, while **Alphabet -3.18%, Salesforce -3.01% and Nike -2.15%** led the index lower and **Chevron +2.47%** led the handful of gainers alongside IBM and Boeing.
items.why: Launch events reliably produce a sell-the-news dip, but the wider tape was pure rates-and-oil rotation: energy bid on $101 Brent while software and consumer names were marked down against a 4.84% discount rate.

items.detail: Gold reversed Tuesday's slide rather than extending it — futures opened at **$4,399, down 0.9%**, then recovered through the session to **$4,435.60**, with spot back **above $4,390 (+1.0%)**.
items.why: A softer dollar let the inflation-hedge bid reassert itself, so the metal stopped trading as a pure real-rates casualty and started pricing the Middle East supply shock as a genuine risk event again.

items.detail: The first of the two prints lands this morning — **August PPI is released at 8:30am ET Thursday**, against a July report that was flat month-on-month but still **+4.7% year-on-year** with **final-demand energy up 18.2%**; CME FedWatch has a September 16 hike at roughly **56%**.

Wednesday's morning weakness turned into the worst session in months — the **Sensex closed down 813.35 points (1.08%) at 74,764.23** and the **Nifty 50 fell 203.60 points (0.86%) to 23,431.50**, its sharpest one-day drop in more than two months and lowest close since **June 11**.
items.why: Brent tagging $100 on the US-Iran tanker exchange hit an oil-importing market that was already contending with a sliding rupee and renewed foreign selling, and the index closed at the day's low after an afternoon recovery attempt failed.

items.detail: The rupee broke to a **record low of ₹95.2250 per dollar** before recovering to settle at **₹95.1050** — a full rupee weaker than Tuesday's ₹94.61 — after traders reported RBI intervention.
items.why: India needs progressively more dollars to fund an energy import bill priced off $100 crude, and that demand combined with dollar outflows overwhelmed the central bank's selling, which now only slows the move rather than stopping it.

items.detail: Thursday opened green but could not hold it — **GIFT Nifty pointed to a positive start**, the **Nifty opened up 11 points at 23,442.50**, and by mid-morning the Sensex was flat with the Nifty back **around 23,400** as auto and IT shares underperformed.
items.why: The index entered the session with RSI in oversold territory, which drew a technical bounce, but elevated crude and rising US bond yields capped it immediately.

items.detail: The selling broadened well beyond the headline index — **36 of the 50 Nifty constituents fell**, NSE breadth was **2,092 decliners to 1,481 advancers**, and the **MidCap and SmallCap indices lost 0.51% and 0.48%**, with **Infosys, HCL Technologies and Tech Mahindra** the top Nifty losers while metal and pharma stayed bid.
items.why: Nifty IT remained the single biggest drag for a third session as higher US rate-hike odds squeeze the client technology budgets services exporters depend on, while metals benefit from the commodity move and pharma from weaker-rupee export realisations.

items.detail: Domestic money is still absorbing the foreign exit, but the gap narrowed — **FPIs sold ₹582.99 crore** on September 9 while **DIIs bought ₹1,509.04 crore**.
items.why: Foreign selling is being driven by the rupee and the Fed rather than by Indian fundamentals, so domestic institutions with rupee liabilities are willing to take the other side, which is why the fall has been orderly rather than a rout despite three straight down sessions.

items.detail: The $78,000 shelf flagged yesterday is holding, but only just — **Bitcoin trades at $78,039, down 1%** on the day with $35.2 billion of volume and a $1.57 trillion market cap, while **Ethereum is at $2,458.15, down 1.5%**.
items.why: Brent above $100 and a 10-year yield at 4.841% keep September rate-hike odds near 56%, and crypto is trading as a straight duration-sensitive risk asset into Thursday's PPI rather than as a geopolitical hedge.

items.detail: The forced selling is decelerating rather than accelerating — **$238.60 million of liquidations across 81,106 traders** in the last 24 hours, down from Tuesday's $264 million, with **open interest at $52.97 billion, up 14% on the month**.
items.why: Two consecutive days of long flushes have already cleared the densest leverage clusters above $78,000, so each subsequent leg lower is finding fewer positions to cascade through, but the elevated open interest means the risk has been reduced rather than removed.

items.detail: The single biggest crypto event of next week is now regulatory, not monetary — Senate Majority Leader John Thune has filed cloture setting up a **September 15 vote on the CLARITY Act**, which needs **60 votes** to advance, one day before the FOMC decision.
items.why: Seven Democratic senators have said the current draft falls short on ethics, consumer protection and illicit finance, and with only 14 working days before the October recess a failed cloture vote would effectively kill the bill for 2026 — Polymarket odds of passage have collapsed from 82% in February to about 16%, with Galaxy Digital at 10%.

items.detail: Fund flows are now openly selective rather than broadly risk-off — **Bitcoin ETFs drew $986.9 million in the week to September 4** while Ethereum, Solana and XRP funds all saw inflows shrink, with **XRP ETF assets up 28% to $1.51 billion** and **Solana products leading 2026 growth at 33%**.
items.why: Institutional allocators are treating Bitcoin as the macro-hedge sleeve and the altcoin funds as discretionary add-ons, so when rate-hike odds rise the marginal dollar concentrates in BTC rather than leaving the asset class entirely.

items.detail: The month-long recovery is broader than the past week suggests — **XRP and Solana are each up roughly 39% from their August lows** and Bitcoin is **up 21.9% over 30 days**, yet all four majors including Ethereum remain **negative for 2026**.
items.why: August's rebound repaired a first-half drawdown rather than starting a new advance, so the assets that fell furthest earlier in the year have bounced hardest without closing the year-to-date gap, leaving Bitcoin with the shortest distance back to breakeven.

crossCuttingTheme: The Gulf conflict escalated from proxy strikes to a direct US-Iran naval exchange — US forces hit five Iranian tankers at Kharg Island and Tehran claimed attacks on two American vessels and eight tankers — pushing Brent 3.4% higher to $101.21 and driving the 10-year Treasury yield to 4.841%, its highest since November 2023, a move amplified by a Treasury buyback that came in at $6 billion when the market wanted $7-10 billion; that single rates impulse took the S&P 500 to 7,636.46 with the Russell 2000 off 1.30%, the Nifty to its lowest close since June at 23,431.50, the rupee to a record ₹95.2250, and Bitcoin to a fragile $78,039 — with this morning's August PPI the first of two prints that decide whether the Fed hikes on September 16.
